beats.say: Sunlight looks white, but it's really a mix of every color traveling together. Think of it as a bundle of waves, some long and red, some short and blue.
beats.visual: Draw the sun at left with a bundle of wavy lines leaving it to the right: a long stretched red wave on top, a tight short blue wave on the bottom, labeled 'white light'.

adds.what: bundle of colored waves, long red to short blue

beats.section: Sunlight is a mix of colors with different wavelengths

beats.say: Look at these two waves. The red one has a long wavelength, the blue one a short wavelength. That difference in size is the one idea everything hangs on today.
beats.visual: Highlight the red and blue waves in the bundle, contrasting their spacing.

beats.say: Now picture that bundle hitting air. Air is mostly tiny nitrogen and oxygen molecules, far smaller than any of these light waves.
beats.visual: Draw a scatter of small circles to the right of the waves labeled 'air molecules', with the wave bundle arrow pointing into them.

adds.what: cluster of tiny air molecule circles

beats.say: So we have long red waves, short blue waves, and tiny molecules in the way. Does that picture of light and air make sense so far?
beats.bridge: Okay, now let's zoom in on one molecule.

beats.say: Here's one molecule. When light passes, its electric field shakes the molecule's electrons, and those shaking electrons send light back out in new directions. That's called scattering.
beats.visual: Draw one big circle in the center labeled 'molecule', an incoming wave from the left, and short arrows spraying outward in every direction labeled 'scattered'.

adds.what: arrows radiating out in all directions

beats.section: Air molecules scatter short blue light much more than red

beats.say: The key is how strongly it scatters. It's called Rayleigh scattering, and it goes as one over wavelength to the fourth power. Shorter waves scatter enormously more.
beats.visual: Above the molecule, write 'scattering ∝ 1 / λ⁴' labeled 'Rayleigh'.

adds.what: equation: scattering proportional to one over wavelength to the fourth

beats.say: That fourth power is what makes this so lopsided. Halve the wavelength and the scattering jumps sixteen times. Is the idea of scattering clicking for you?
beats.visual: Highlight the exponent four in the equation.
beats.bridge: Good, let's put real numbers on it.

beats.say: Blue light is about four hundred fifty nanometers long. Red light is about seven hundred nanometers. Let's compare them as bars.
beats.visual: Draw two vertical bars, a shorter blue bar labeled '450 nm' and a taller red bar labeled '700 nm', titled 'wavelength'.

adds.what: bar chart: blue 450 nanometers, red 700 nanometers

beats.section: Real numbers show blue scatters about six times more

beats.say: Seven hundred divided by four hundred fifty is about one and a half. Raise that to the fourth power and you get roughly six.
beats.visual: Write '(700/450)⁴ ≈ 6' to the right of the bars, arrow from the bars to it.

adds.what: calculation 700 over 450, to the fourth, about 6

beats.say: So blue light gets scattered about six times more than red. That scattered blue comes at your eyes from every direction of the sky. Does that number make sense?
beats.bridge: Now here's the puzzle most people miss.

beats.say: Violet light is even shorter than blue, so it scatters even more. So why isn't the sky violet? Picture the sunlight spectrum as a curve.
beats.visual: Draw a plot with color on the horizontal axis from violet to red and a curve that is low at violet and peaks in the middle, labeled 'sunlight'.

adds.what: plot of sunlight brightness across colors, low at violet

beats.section: Why the sky isn't violet: sun and eyes

beats.say: First, the sun simply sends less violet, see how low the curve starts. Second, our eyes are much less sensitive to violet.
beats.visual: Highlight the low violet end of the sunlight curve.

beats.say: Our color sensors blend all that scattered blue and violet, plus a bit of green, into the sky blue we actually perceive.
beats.visual: Draw an eye to the right of the plot with an arrow from the violet and blue part of the curve into it, labeled 'looks blue'.
beats.bridge: Great, let's pull it all together.

beats.say: So, sunlight is a mix of wavelengths. Tiny air molecules scatter short waves far more, about six times more for blue than red. Our eyes and the sun's output make it blue, not violet.
beats.section: Recap: wavelength, scattering, and our eyes

beats.say: And as a bonus, at sunset light crosses far more air, the blue gets scattered away before reaching you, and the reds left over paint the sky.
